blocks.text: Quick verdict

ProxyEmpire is the better choice for small and irregular workloads, especially US-focused ones: $3.50/GB at entry against $5/GB on SOAX's Sandbox for US traffic, and its prepaid traffic never expires while SOAX credits lapse after 60 days. SOAX is the better choice for larger mobile-first and ad-verification teams: its network is several times bigger (155M residential plus 33M mobile), it supports UDP and QUIC, and its Team and Scale plans plus Tier 3 country rates can undercut ProxyEmpire at volume.

SOAX and ProxyEmpire are both strong in residential and mobile proxies and both include ISP targeting. They differ sharply in how they bill. SOAX uses prepaid credits whose per-GB cost depends on your plan and the exit country, and those credits expire after 60 days. ProxyEmpire uses straightforward per-GB tiers and lets prepaid traffic roll over forever. This comparison looks at network size, protocols and real costs for US-focused and global workloads.

blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX rebuilt its pricing in 2026 around credits and country tiers. Residential and mobile traffic share one balance and one per-GB rate, and the rate depends on your plan and the country your exit IP is in: US and German traffic costs more than Indian or Filipino traffic. SOAX advertises 155 million residential and 33 million mobile IPs in 195 countries, supports UDP and QUIC as well as SOCKS5, and includes city and ISP targeting on every plan. It discontinued its datacenter and ISP proxies between late 2025 and mid 2026.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire is a Bulgarian-registered provider (SWIFT SAAS LTD) that has been selling since 2020. Its residential and mobile networks share one system with 30M+ advertised IPs in 170+ countries, and country, region, city and ISP targeting are included at no extra cost. The standout policy is bandwidth rollover: prepaid traffic carries forward indefinitely, even after a subscription lapses. Proxyway's 2026 market tests found ProxyEmpire's pool was the third largest among the providers it tested.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: SOAX vs ProxyEmpire

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

At 10 GB a month, ProxyEmpire is the cheaper option at about $35 against $50 for SOAX, roughly 30% less. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; SOAX comes to about $300. Look past the per-GB figure too. ProxyEmpire lets unused traffic carry forward, while SOAX's allowance does not (credits expire 60 days after they are added). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, SOAX (155M residential + 33M mobile) is about 5.2x larger than ProxyEmpire (30M+). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, SOAX lists 195 countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes, and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. With ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: city and ISP targeting for local results. How ProxyEmpire compares: Google was its weakest target in independent tests.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. How ProxyEmpire compares: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: granular location filters. With ProxyEmpire: free city and ISP targeting. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. How ProxyEmpire compares: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost.

Tight budgets: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. The limitation on the SOAX side: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test SOAX and ProxyEmpire before you commit
The quickest way to choose between SOAX and ProxyEmpire is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).

2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day. 3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, SOAX comes out ahead in 3, ProxyEmpire in 1, and 2 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
